topic: Self-massage with a ball: a 5-minute routine

slides.headline: Got a tennis ball? You've got a routine
slides.sub: Five minutes, four spots, one ball. Handy between massage appointments.

slides.title: Minute 1: feet
slides.body: Stand and roll the sole of one foot over the ball from heel to toes with gentle pressure, about thirty seconds each side. A nice reset for feet after long days in shoes or thongs.

slides.title: Minute 2: calves
slides.body: Sit on the floor with the ball under one calf. Slowly roll or rest on tender spots while pointing and flexing your foot. Cross the other leg on top if you want a bit more pressure.

slides.title: Minute 3: glutes
slides.body: Sit on the ball on one side and lean into the fleshy part of your buttock, making small slow circles. Move off anything that feels sharp or sends tingling down the leg.

slides.title: Minutes 4 and 5: upper back
slides.body: Stand with the ball between a shoulder blade and a wall. Lean in and move slowly around the muscles beside the spine, staying off the bony spine itself and away from the front of the neck.

slides.title: Keep it comfortable
slides.body: Aim for pressure around 4 to 6 out of 10 that eases as you go. Skip areas with bruising, varicose veins, a recent injury or numbness, and stop if symptoms start spreading.

slides.headline: Want help with the tricky spots?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists can work the areas a ball can't reach and suggest what to roll at home between visits. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
All you need for this five-minute routine is a tennis ball and a wall.

Start with the soles of your feet, then calves, then glutes, and finish with two minutes on the upper back against a wall. Go slowly, breathe out, and keep the pressure moderate. It should ease as you go, not build.

Self-massage is a nice way to take the edge off tightness between appointments. It won't replace movement or strength work, but it can make both feel a bit easier.

Skip bruised areas, varicose veins, fresh injuries or anywhere that feels numb, and stop if tingling or pain starts to spread.

story.headline: Five minutes, one tennis ball
story.body: Feet, calves, glutes, then upper back against a wall. Moderate pressure that eases as you go.
